- When sentiment is strongly positive (≥0.7) and forecast shows sharp downward drift, reduce the forecast slope to avoid overcorrection.  
- If recent price history shows a spike followed by a sharp drop, model tends to overshoot downward — adjust forecast to flatten the dip and allow mean reversion.  
- When sentiment is negative (≤0.3) and forecast is overly optimistic, reduce forecast by 5–10% to reflect bearish sentiment.  
- For 30-day forecasts, if the last 3–5 days of history show strong downward momentum, model often underestimates the drop — increase forecast by 2–5% to account for lagged momentum.  
- If sentiment is volatile (alternating +/–0.3) and forecast is smooth, introduce slight volatility in forecast to match sentiment noise.  
- When sentiment is neutral (0.3–0.7) and forecast is consistently above true outcome, apply a downward bias correction of 1–3% to reflect mean reversion.  
- For forecasts with early high values followed by low true values, reduce forecast by 3–5% in the first 5–7 days to avoid premature peak.
